newsitem.title: INDIA: NatWest's Sethi reaction to India political flux.
newsitem.headline: NatWest's Sethi reaction to India political flux.

text.p: Alok Sethi, director of NatWest Markets, on Saturday gave Reuters the following view on Indian markets after the United Front alliance was defeated in a confidence motion and a search for a new coalition got underway.
He said the political situation was in a state of flux and the outcome was too difficult to call at the moment, but he believed a snap election could be avoided.
"It is a game of coalitions. And up until this moment it is difficult to know what the outcome will be. But the overall impression is that they will work something out."
He said he was not unduly worried by the prospect of an election, provided a party emerged with a clear mandate from the vote.
He said the progress of coalition talks could be hindered by the budget proposals, which are pending approval in a special session of parliament set for April 21-23.
"They really don't want to ruffle any feathers ahead of the budget approval.
SLOWDOWN IN DECISION TAKING FROM DELHI
Regardless of whether another coalition is formed or mid-term elections are called, Sethi said he foresaw a serious slowdown in decision-taking from New Delhi.

He expected a decision on oil product price rises to be stalled, leaving refiners still owed billions of rupees from the oil pool deficit -- the mechanism used to finance India's cross-subsidy system for petroleum products.

Plans to announce a restructuring of the oil sector will also be left on hold. And in the power sector he expected some project approvals, and post-approval financial closures to be left hanging. There will be an impact on the entire infrastructure, which is already under strain, he said.
Foreign direct investors will probably watch and wait before making commitments, and foreign institutional investors (FIIs) will have a wider window of opportunity to buy into India at these prices.

Sethi said he expected the market has largely written in expectations that Finance Minister P. Chidambaram's budget proposals will be passed, but will still draw some extra strength once parliament gives its approval.
But political uncertainty, slow economic turnaround and low business confidence would weigh on sentiment.
"The downside risk exists quite a bit. I don't see FIIs chasing prices and moving them higher."

He said the Bombay Stock Exchange top 30 share index could reach 3,650 to 3,700 once the budget sets in. On the downside it could sink to between 3,100 to 3,200 as pessimism sets in the event mid-term polls are called.
